==Problem==
In an equiangular hexagon, all interior angles measure <imath>120^\circ</imath>. An example of such a hexagon with side lengths <imath>2</imath>, <imath>3</imath>, <imath>1</imath>, <imath>3</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, and <imath>2</imath> is shown below, inscribed in equilateral triangle <imath>ABC</imath>. Consider all equiangular hexagons with positive integer side lengths that can be inscribed in <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>, with all six vertices on the sides of the triangle. What is the total number of such hexagons? Hexagons that differ only by a rotation or a reflection are considered the same.

<asy>
defaultpen(linewidth(0.8)); size(5cm); dotfactor = 5.5; pair A = 6 * dir(210), B = 6 * dir(330), C = 6 * dir(90), U = (2C + A)/3, V = (5A + C)/6, W = (5A + B)/6, X = (2B + A)/3, Y = (2B + C)/3, Z = (2C + B)/3; fill(U--V--W--X--Y--Z--cycle, gray(0.8)); draw(A--B--C--cycle^^U--Z^^V--W^^X--Y); label("$A$", A, dir(A)); label("$B$", B, dir(B)); label("$C$", C, dir(C)); label("$1$", (V + W)/2, dir(195)/2); label("$3$", (W + X)/2, dir(270)/2); label("$2$", (X + Y)/2, dir(330)/2); label("$2$", (Y + Z)/2, dir(30)/2); label("$2$", (Z + U)/2, dir(90)/2); label("$3$", (U + V)/2, dir(150)/2); dot(U); dot(V); dot(W); dot(X); dot(Y); dot(Z);
</asy>

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 4\qquad\textbf{(B) } 5\qquad\textbf{(C) } 6\qquad\textbf{(D) } 7\qquad\textbf{(E) } 8</imath>



==Remark== 

Note that the original solution designated as "Solution 3" has been removed due to redundancy.

==Solution 1 (Recursion)==

Let the side lengths of the hexagon be <imath> a, b, c, d, e, f </imath>. Obviously, each one of these is to be in between 1, 2, or 3 (see solution 2 for proof). Every 2 can be followed by a 2 or a 3. Every 3 must be followed by a 1 or 2, and every 1 must be followed by a 3. The question is now how many strings of length 6 satisfy these conditions, in which the first and last numbers also satisfy these conditions.

To count that, we use recursion. Let <imath> a_n </imath> be a string of length <imath> n </imath> ending in 1, <imath> b_n </imath> is a string of length <imath> n </imath> ending in 2, and <imath> c_n </imath> is a string that ends in 3. For <imath> a_{n+1} </imath>, we have that it must come from <imath> c_n </imath>, so <imath> a_{n+1} = c_n </imath>. Additionally, <imath> b_{n+1} = b_n + c_n </imath>, and <imath> c_{n+1} = a_n </imath>. Then, <imath> a_1 = 1 </imath>, <imath> b_1 = 1 </imath>, and <imath> c_1 = 1 </imath>. Thus, <imath> a_2 = 1 </imath>, <imath> b_2 = 2 </imath>, and <imath> c_2 = 1 </imath>; <imath> a_3 = 1 </imath>, <imath> b_3 = 3 </imath>, and <imath> c_3 = 1 </imath>; <imath> a_4 = 1 </imath>, <imath> b_4 = 4 </imath>, <imath> c_4 = 1 </imath>; <imath> a_5 = 1 </imath>, <imath> b_5 = 5 </imath>, <imath> c_5 = 1 </imath>; and finally <imath> a_6 = 1 </imath>, <imath> b_6 = 6 </imath>, and <imath> c_6 = 1 </imath>.

Our answer is <imath> a_6 + b_6 + c_6 </imath>, or <imath> 1+6+1 = \boxed{8} </imath>.

~Pinotation

~HeirX on TT - Minor edits

==Solution 2==
An equiangular hexagon has all interior angles <imath>120^\circ</imath>, so consecutive sides turn by <imath>60^\circ</imath> each time.
Place an equilateral triangle <imath>ABC</imath> of side length <imath>6</imath> (this is the side length in the given example since
<imath>1+3+2=6</imath> along each side).

Since all six vertices of the hexagon lie on the sides of <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>, each side of <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>
contains exactly two consecutive vertices of the hexagon. Hence three alternating sides of the hexagon lie
along the sides of <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>.

Look near vertex <imath>A</imath>.
Between the two sides <imath>AB,AC</imath> and the hexagon there is a triangular gap whose vertex is <imath>A</imath>.
Because <imath>\angle A=60^\circ</imath> and the hexagon makes <imath>120^\circ</imath> interior angles, each of the two angles of the gap
adjacent to the hexagon is <imath>60^\circ</imath>. Therefore the gap at <imath>A</imath> is an equilateral triangle.
Do the same at <imath>B</imath> and <imath>C</imath>: the hexagon is obtained by ``cutting off'' three equilateral corner triangles.

Let the side lengths of the three cut-off equilateral triangles at <imath>A,B,C</imath> be
<cmath>
x,\ y,\ z \quad (\text{positive integers}).
</cmath>
Along side <imath>AB</imath> of length <imath>6</imath>, the two cuts remove lengths <imath>x</imath> (near <imath>A</imath>) and <imath>y</imath> (near <imath>B</imath>),
so the remaining middle segment on <imath>AB</imath> (which is a side of the hexagon) has length <imath>6-x-y</imath>.
Similarly the other two middle segments on <imath>BC</imath> and <imath>CA</imath> have lengths <imath>6-y-z</imath> and <imath>6-z-x</imath>.

Thus, going around the hexagon, its six side lengths are
<cmath>
(6-x-y,\ y,\ 6-y-z,\ z,\ 6-z-x,\ x),
</cmath>
so all are positive if
<cmath>
x+y\le 5,\qquad y+z\le 5,\qquad z+x\le 5,
</cmath>
with <imath>x,y,z\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}</imath>.

Two such hexagons that differ by a rotation or reflection of the equilateral triangle correspond exactly
to permuting <imath>(x,y,z)</imath>, so we count solutions up to permutation. We may assume
<cmath>
1\le x\le y\le z.
</cmath>

Now enumerate all triples <imath>(x,y,z)</imath> with <imath>x\le y\le z</imath> satisfying the pair-sum constraints.

If <imath>x=1</imath>, then <imath>1+y\le 5\Rightarrow y\le 4</imath> and <imath>1+z\le 5\Rightarrow z\le 4</imath>.
Also <imath>y+z\le 5</imath>.
The valid triples are:
<cmath>
(1,1,1),\ (1,1,2),\ (1,1,3),\ (1,1,4),\ (1,2,2),\ (1,2,3).
</cmath>
(For example, <imath>(1,2,4)</imath> fails since <imath>2+4>5</imath>.)

If <imath>x=2</imath>, then <imath>2+y\le 5\Rightarrow y\le 3</imath> and <imath>2+z\le 5\Rightarrow z\le 3</imath>.
Also <imath>y\le z</imath> and <imath>y+z\le 5</imath>.
The valid triples are:
<cmath>
(2,2,2),\ (2,2,3).
</cmath>

If <imath>x\ge 3</imath>, then <imath>x+y\ge 3+3=6>5</imath>, impossible.

So there are
<cmath>
6+2=8
</cmath>
unordered triples, hence <imath>8</imath> distinct hexagons up to rotation/reflection.

<imath>\boxed{8}</imath>

~ Shreyan of Winston Churchill Middle School

~Pinotation (Formatting)


==Solution 3 (Casework)==

We can already get <imath>(1,1,1)</imath> and <imath>(2,2,2)</imath> if we want equal sides (the case <imath>(3,3,3)</imath> doesn't work as it makes a triangle)

Then, we can compute <imath>(1,1,2)</imath>, <imath>(2,2,3)</imath>, <imath>(2,2,1)</imath>, <imath>(1,1,4)</imath>, <imath>(1,1,3)</imath> for cases of the same side length (and also two of the same)

Finally, we find the cause <imath>(1,2,3)</imath> for all unique numbers.

This gives us a total of <imath>\fbox{(E)\ 8}</imath> total cases.

~Namish Dour

==Solution 4 (Burnside's Lemma, unnecessarily long)==

Let <imath>X</imath> be the set of all possible orientations of the hexagon (where reflections and rotations are different), let <imath>\mathcal{O}</imath> denote the set of all orbits of <imath>X</imath> under <imath>D_3</imath> where <imath>D_3</imath> is the dihedral group of order <imath>3</imath>. Burnside's tells us that <cmath>|\mathcal{O}| = \frac{1}{|D_3|}\sum_{g \in D_3} |\text{Fix}(g)|</cmath> where <imath>\text{Fix}(g) = \{x \mid g \cdot x = x\}</imath>, the fixed points under the action <imath>g</imath>. <imath>|\mathcal{O}|</imath> is the solution to our problem in this case, as every rotation or reflection of the hexagon is represented in <imath>D_3</imath>. More accurately, <imath>D_3</imath> represents the symmetries of the triangle, and the hexagon is the triangle with the vertices cut out.

First, let's find <imath>|X|</imath>. Letting the sides of the hexagon be <imath>a,b,c,d,e,f</imath>, we note that <imath>b=6-a-c</imath>,<imath>d=6-c-e</imath>,<imath>f=6-e-a</imath>. Since <imath>0<a,b,c,d,e,f<6</imath>, <imath>1\leq a+c,c+e,e+a\leq 5</imath>. We can now do casework:

<imath>a=1</imath>:
We have <imath>1 \leq c \leq 4</imath>, <imath>1 \leq e \leq 4</imath>, and <imath>1 \leq c+e \leq 5</imath>. Letting <imath>x=c</imath> and <imath>y=e</imath>, we manually check the lattice points in a square in the <imath>xy</imath>-plane with coordinates <imath>(1,1)</imath> to <imath>(4,4)</imath> for <imath>x+y > 5</imath>. <imath>6</imath> elements satisfy this inequality, so they are the solutions <imath>(c,e)</imath> which don't work - therefore, there are <imath>16-6=10</imath> working solutions <imath>(c,e)</imath> satisfying our inequalities.

<imath>a=2</imath>:
<imath>1 \leq c \leq 3</imath>, <imath>1 \leq e \leq 3</imath>, <imath>1 \leq c+e \leq 5</imath>. In a similar fashion, in the <imath>3 \times 3</imath> square of lattice points only <imath>(3,3)</imath> fails to meet <imath>c+e\leq 5</imath> so <imath>8</imath> solutions work from here.

<imath>a=3</imath>:
<imath>1 \leq c \leq 2</imath>, <imath>1 \leq e \leq 2</imath>, <imath>1 \leq c+e \leq 5</imath>. Obviously every solution works here, so <imath>4</imath> solutions add to the count.

<imath>a=4</imath>:
Here, <imath>(c,e)=(1,1)</imath> is the only working solution.

The final count is <imath>23</imath>. Therefore, <imath>|X|=23</imath>.


There are three conjugacy classes of <imath>D_3</imath>: <imath>\{e\},\{R,R^{-1}\},</imath> and <imath>\{T,TR,TR^2\}</imath>. We picture <imath>D_3</imath> as a triangle with each of the vertices labeled <imath>a,c,e</imath> in some order. (The hexagon is the equilateral triangle of side 6 with smaller equilateral triangles of length <imath>a,c,e</imath> cut out of the corners. <imath>\text{Fix}(g)=\text{Fix}(h)</imath> if <imath>g</imath> and <imath>h</imath> are in the same conjugacy class, so it suffices to find <imath>|\text{Fix}(e)|</imath>, <imath>|\text{Fix}(R)|</imath>, and <imath>|\text{Fix}(T)|</imath>. 

Every "vertex" is in its own orbit after the <imath>e</imath>-action, meaning that every element is completely fixed, so <imath>|\text{Fix}(e)=|X|</imath>. 

The orbit of <imath>R</imath> contains all the vertices, meaning for an element to be fixed, every vertex must be the same, resulting in two triangles: <imath>(1,1,1)</imath> and <imath>(2,2,2)</imath>. 

Finally, the <imath>T</imath>-action fixes one of the vertices and swaps the other two. WLOG let <imath>a</imath> be the fixed vertex and <imath>{c,e}</imath> be swapped - meaning that they must be equal for the triangle to be fixed. Our equations become <imath>1 \leq a+c \leq 5</imath>, <imath>1 \leq 2c \leq 5</imath>, or that <imath>c \in {1,2}</imath>. <imath>c=1</imath> generates <imath>4</imath> solutions, while <imath>c=2</imath> generates <imath>3</imath>. Therefore, <imath>7</imath> triangles are fixed by the <imath>T</imath>-action, and <imath>|\text{Fix}(T)|=7</imath>.

Plugging all this into Burnside's, 
\begin{align*}
|\mathcal{O}| &= \frac{1}{|D_3|}\sum_{g \in D_3} |\text{Fix}(g)| \\
|\mathcal{O}| &= \frac{1}{6}(1 \cdot 23+2 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 7) \\
|\mathcal{O}| &= \frac{1}{6}(48) \\
|\mathcal{O}| &= \fbox{(E) 8}.
\end{align*}

~Moonwatcher22

==Solution 5 (Intuitive, Simple)==

Observe that the side length of <imath>\triangle ABC</imath> is <imath>6</imath>. A hexagon is equiangular 
if and only if all ``outer triangles,'' formed by two adjacent vertices of the 
hexagon and one vertex of the equilateral triangle, are equilateral. We perform 
casework on each equilateral triangle and obtain <imath>8</imath> different configurations. 
Hence <imath>\boxed{8}</imath>.
